This module of the [companion curriculum](index.qmd) is about R, the language in which the analysis of the course is written, as the EU-frames case uses it. The first steps in R, from the console and the script to objects, data frames, the pipe, the datawizard verbs, a first table and a first figure, are taught in [Getting started with R](https://codemoreh.github.io/ar4ds/tools/r.html) on the umbrella site of the course, a module that assumes no programming at all and works on the data of the housing-audit case, a file small enough to look at whole, with an outcome that is either yes or no. This page assumes those steps and takes the tools to the country-year panel of the EU-frames case, a table of 270 rows built from Eurobarometer surveys: the files of the case and the routes by which they arrive, the grammar of graphics in depth, and the specification curve of the case.

The panel is the material for two things that a file of yes-or-no outcomes cannot show. A scatterplot with a fitted line needs measures that vary continuously, and the panel holds them, among them the unemployment rate and the mean score with which the respondents of a country-year framed the EU in cosmopolitan terms. The curve of the case mixes predictors whose results point in opposite directions, so it has to be aligned with the claim before it can be read.

The code of sections 2 and 3 is shown without being run, because it reads the panel of the case, which is on your machine once you have the workspace, and the numbers quoted in section 3 are computed from the curve of the case when the page is built. The way to learn is still to type. Copy each block into the workspace that you downloaded from the [setup page](https://codemoreh.github.io/ar4ds/setup.html#the-workspace) and run it there.

The courses use the module at several points. It is the companion of the R tutorial in Part 2 of the [one-day course on data tools](../tracks/eu-frames-one-day-data-tools/part-2.qmd) and of the first session of [day 2](../tracks/eu-frames-three-days/day-2.qmd) of the three-day course.

## 1. Other formats, and fetching data {#sec-formats}

The panel and the curve of the case are CSV files, read as [section 6 of Getting started with R](https://codemoreh.github.io/ar4ds/tools/r.html#sec-reading) reads the housing-audit file. The Eurobarometer waves from which the panel was built arrive from the GESIS archive in another format, as files in the format of Stata, a statistical package, with value labels on their answer codes. [Section 13](https://codemoreh.github.io/ar4ds/tools/r-further.html#sec-formats) of the second part of that module reads a file of this kind in the browser, with its labels, and covers the other formats in which data arrive, from Excel workbooks to Parquet files. The [data management module](data-management.qmd#sec-build) builds the respondent file of this case from the Stata files of the waves.

The data of the case arrive by three routes, and the [subsection on fetching data](https://codemoreh.github.io/ar4ds/tools/r-further.html#sec-fetching) in the same part introduces the package for each. The panel is fetched from the Open Science Framework by the script `R/get_data.R` in the workspace of the case, which uses the osfr package. The macro variables of the panel were obtained from the World Bank with the WDI package, which queries the indicators of the World Bank by their codes, as [section 3.2](data-sources.qmd#sec-worldbank) of the data sources module sets out. The Eurobarometer waves come from the GESIS archive, which offers no interface through which a program could download them, so the course downloads the waves by hand, as [section 3.1](data-sources.qmd#sec-gesis) of the same module shows step by step.

## 2. The grammar of graphics {#sec-grammar}

[Section 12 of Getting started with R](https://codemoreh.github.io/ar4ds/tools/r.html#sec-figure) draws a first figure, and this section takes the grammar further on the panel of the EU-frames case, read as `euframes <- readr::read_csv("data/EUframes_cy.csv")` in the workspace of the case. Its 270 rows are 27 countries in each of ten years, and its columns include the unemployment rate (`unemp`), the mean score of cosmopolitan framing of the EU among the respondents of each country-year (`mcosmo`, from 0 to 1) and whether an EU or IMF assistance programme was running (`bailout`), so it has the continuous measures that a scatterplot, a fitted line and a panel for each country need. **ggplot2**, a member of the tidyverse family of packages, is the one that draws [@WickhamEtAl2019WelcomeTidyverse]. Almost every chart on the pages and slides of the course is built with it, so reading ggplot2 code is how you satisfy yourself that a figure shows what its caption says it shows. The figures that you draw yourself, in the workspaces and the browser labs, and the live class chart on the multiverse page of the case, are drawn with tinyplot ([section 12 of Getting started with R](https://codemoreh.github.io/ar4ds/tools/r.html#sec-figure)), which is light enough to run in a browser. The other exceptions are the main chart of the [Multiverse page](../cases/eu-frames/multiverse.qmd) of the EU-frames case, which a script of the course draws in the browser, the charts of the [decision map](../cases/eu-frames/map.qmd), which Observable Plot draws, and a few figures in the methods modules that packages with plotting functions of their own draw.

The name abbreviates 'the grammar of graphics', the idea that any chart can be described as a combination of a few standard parts, much as a grammar describes how words combine into sentences. ggplot2 therefore has no separate function for each chart type. It splits a figure into parts that recombine freely: the data, the mapping from columns to visual properties, the geometric shapes drawn, the scales that decide what those shapes look like, the panels that the plot is divided into, and last the labels and the styling. A scatterplot and a bar chart are two fillings of the same slots, and once you know the slots you can read the figures on this site, including kinds you have not met yet.

### Data, mapping and geometry

A plot needs data, a mapping, and at least one geom. Everything else has a default good enough to start with.

```r
ggplot2::ggplot(euframes, ggplot2::aes(x = unemp, y = mcosmo)) +
  ggplot2::geom_point()
```

Three things happen there. `ggplot()` receives the data frame and declares which columns drive the picture. `aes()` is the **aesthetic mapping**, and it states that the unemployment rate governs horizontal position while the cosmopolitan-framing score governs vertical position. `geom_point()` adds a **geom**, a layer of geometric shapes, drawing one point per row – 270 points for 270 country-years. Axis ranges, tick marks, gridlines and the panel background are all inferred from the data, which is why this bare version is already a readable figure.

Layers are joined with `+`, never with the pipe `|>`. The reason is historical, since ggplot2 settled on `+` years before R had a native pipe. The practical consequence is that a long chain changes operator exactly once, at the point where it stops reshaping data and starts drawing, and typing `|>` where `+` belongs is among the commonest first-week errors in R.

### Mapping and setting

Every visual property of a layer can be given two ways, and confusing them is the next commonest error. Put a property inside `aes()` and it is **mapped**: its value is read from a column, it varies row by row, and ggplot2 adds a legend explaining the correspondence. Put the same property outside `aes()`, as an ordinary argument to the geom, and it is **set**, taking one fixed value for the whole layer, with no legend because there is nothing to explain.

```r
# MAPPED: colour comes from a column, so the points differ and a legend appears
ggplot2::ggplot(euframes, ggplot2::aes(x = unemp, y = mcosmo, colour = factor(bailout))) +
  ggplot2::geom_point()

# SET: colour is a constant, identical for every point, and no legend appears
ggplot2::ggplot(euframes, ggplot2::aes(x = unemp, y = mcosmo)) +
  ggplot2::geom_point(colour = "#0e3b6a", alpha = 0.5)
```

`alpha` controls opacity, running from 0 for invisible to 1 for solid, and setting it below 1 is the standard remedy for a scatterplot where points pile up on one another. The constant `"#0e3b6a"` is a hex colour code, the dark blue that the course figures use.

Leaving out the `factor()` wrapped around `bailout` produces the wrong figure without any warning. `bailout` is stored as 0 and 1 in numeric form, so `colour = bailout` gives ggplot2 a number, which it treats as continuous, drawing a colour gradient and a legend running smoothly from 0.00 to 1.00. What you wanted was two categories in two colours, and `factor(bailout)` is how you say so. The same applies to `year`, which is also numeric: map it raw for a gradient across the decade, or wrap it in `factor()` for ten discrete groups.

### Layers

A figure can have as many layers as you need, each with its own geom, and they are drawn in the order written, so later layers cover earlier ones.

```r
ggplot2::ggplot(euframes, ggplot2::aes(x = unemp, y = mcosmo)) +
  ggplot2::geom_point(alpha = 0.4, colour = "#848c94") +
  ggplot2::geom_smooth(method = "lm", colour = "#0e3b6a", fill = "#0e3b6a", alpha = 0.15)
```

The grey points are drawn first and the trend line over them. `geom_smooth()` fits a line through the cloud and draws it with a band showing the uncertainty around it, and `method = "lm"` asks for a straight line from the same least-squares method that the statistical methods module uses to fit models. R then prints the message `` `geom_smooth()` using formula = 'y ~ x' ``, which only reports the relationship that was fitted and needs no action. Reference layers behave the same way: `geom_hline(yintercept = 0)` rules a horizontal line at zero, and section 3 uses one to split a figure into results that support a claim and results that do not.

Line thickness is set with `linewidth`, whereas point size and type size are set with `size`, and mixing the two up is behind a great many warnings.

```r
ggplot2::geom_line(linewidth = 0.4)   # the thickness of a drawn line
ggplot2::geom_point(size = 0.7)       # the area of a plotted point
ggplot2::geom_text(size = 3.5)        # the height of a piece of type
```

Passing `size` to a line geom still works, but R warns "Using `size` aesthetic for lines was deprecated in ggplot2 3.4.0. Please use `linewidth` instead." The reason that the two names survive side by side is that `size` on a point means an area and on text a height, neither of which is a line thickness.

### Scales

The mapping says which column drives colour; the **scale** decides which colours it drives, and the same holds for positions, sizes and shapes. Every mapping gets a default scale, and you override it whenever the default is not what a reader needs.

```r
ggplot2::ggplot(euframes, ggplot2::aes(x = unemp, y = mcosmo, colour = factor(bailout))) +
  ggplot2::geom_point(alpha = 0.8) +
  ggplot2::scale_colour_manual(
    name   = "Assistance programme",
    values = c("0" = "#848c94", "1" = "#a10000"),
    labels = c("0" = "none", "1" = "bailout")
  ) +
  ggplot2::scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(0, 30, by = 5))
```

`scale_colour_manual()` names a colour for each level of the variable. Giving `values` and `labels` as *named* vectors, with `"0" = …` rather than a bare pair, means the assignment cannot silently reverse itself if the data ever arrives in a different order. The colours that the course uses throughout are `#0e3b6a` (dark blue), `#E69F00` (orange), `#009E73` (green), `#a10000` (dark red) and `#848c94` (mid grey), with `#c7ccd2` reserved as the muted grey for results that are not statistically significant. The orange and green belong to a palette built to stay distinguishable under the commonest forms of colour vision deficiency, which is why the decks never rest an argument on a red-green contrast alone.

Position scales follow the same override logic, and one of their arguments catches people out. `scale_x_continuous(breaks = …)` decides where the tick marks fall, but the sibling argument `limits` **removes** every row outside the range before any statistic is computed, so a smoother is refitted on whatever rows remain.

```r
p_trend <- ggplot2::ggplot(euframes, ggplot2::aes(x = unemp, y = mcosmo)) +
  ggplot2::geom_point(alpha = 0.4, colour = "#848c94") +
  ggplot2::geom_smooth(method = "lm", colour = "#0e3b6a")

p_trend + ggplot2::scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0.30, 0.50))   # drops rows, then refits
p_trend + ggplot2::coord_cartesian(ylim = c(0.30, 0.50))        # keeps every row, only zooms
```

Run the first of those and R warns "Removed 163 rows containing non-finite outside the scale range (`stat_smooth()`)", and the trend line you are looking at now runs through 107 country-years rather than 270. `coord_cartesian()` zooms the finished figure instead and leaves the computation untouched, so it is the one to use when you only want a closer look.

### Facets

**Faceting** repeats the same plot once per group, on shared axes, so the groups can be compared by eye instead of by disentangling overlapping series. A country-year table suits it well, since each country can have a panel of its own.

```r
ggplot2::ggplot(euframes, ggplot2::aes(x = year, y = mcosmo)) +
  ggplot2::geom_line(colour = "grey55", linewidth = 0.4) +
  ggplot2::geom_point(size = 0.7) +
  ggplot2::facet_wrap(~ cntry, ncol = 6) +
  ggplot2::scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(2004, 2008, 2013))
```

Twenty-seven small panels appear, one per country code, each showing the cosmopolitan-framing series of that country across the decade. The browser lab of the EU-frames case draws the same figure with tinyplot early in the exercise, so that the crisis years are in view before any model is fitted and it is plain how differently the countries move. The `~ cntry` is a one-sided formula, with nothing to the left of the `~`. A model formula, as in `lm()`, uses the same syntax with an outcome written on the left. `ncol` fixes the shape of the grid. Where two grouping variables matter, `facet_grid(rows = vars(a), cols = vars(b))` crosses them into a matrix of panels.

### Labels and themes

Two layers finish a figure. `labs()` supplies the words – axis titles, plot title, subtitle, caption, legend name – and it deserves more care than beginners give it, because a column name such as `mcosmo` means nothing to a reader who has not opened the codebook. The **theme** then governs everything with no data behind it: type size, gridlines, background, the position of the legend.

```r
ggplot2::ggplot(euframes, ggplot2::aes(x = unemp, y = mcosmo)) +
  ggplot2::geom_point(alpha = 0.4, colour = "#848c94") +
  ggplot2::geom_smooth(method = "lm", colour = "#0e3b6a", fill = "#0e3b6a", alpha = 0.15) +
  ggplot2::labs(
    x       = "Unemployment rate (%)",
    y       = "Cosmopolitan framing (mean score, 0–1)",
    title   = "Unemployment and cosmopolitan framing",
    caption = "270 country-years, EU-frames dataset"
  ) +
  ggplot2::theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  ggplot2::theme(
    panel.grid.minor = ggplot2::element_blank(),
    plot.title       = ggplot2::element_text(face = "bold"),
    legend.position  = "top"
  )
```

`theme_minimal()` is the default look across the course, and `base_size` is its most useful argument, scaling every piece of type at once: 9 for a dense panel of small multiples, 12 for a page figure, 15 and upwards for a slide. A bare `theme()` afterwards overrides individual pieces, and the order matters, because a complete theme applied *after* your adjustments would wipe them out. Inside it, `element_blank()` deletes a piece outright, `element_text()` restyles type, and `element_line()` restyles rules and gridlines.

A plot is an ordinary R object, so you can store it under a name, extend it later, and write it to a file:

```r
p <- ggplot2::ggplot(euframes, ggplot2::aes(x = unemp, y = mcosmo)) +
  ggplot2::geom_point(alpha = 0.4, colour = "#848c94") +
  ggplot2::labs(x = "Unemployment rate (%)", y = "Cosmopolitan framing")

p + ggplot2::geom_smooth(method = "lm") + ggplot2::theme_minimal(base_size = 12)

ggplot2::ggsave("figures/framing_unemployment.png", p, width = 7, height = 5, dpi = 300)
```

`ggsave()` takes its dimensions in inches and writes whichever format the file extension names. When you do not name a plot, it saves the last one drawn, which is convenient but can save the wrong figure, so name the object.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Try it

Draw the scatterplot of `unemp` against `mcosmo`, then change one thing at a time and watch what moves. Swap `geom_point()` for `geom_text(aes(label = cntry))` and each point becomes its country code; move `colour = factor(bailout)` from inside `aes()` to outside it and read the error it raises; drop the `factor()` and compare the two legends. Then add `facet_wrap(~ year)` and decide for yourself whether ten panels tell you more than one crowded cloud does.
:::

### From the pipe to the plot

Reshaping and drawing usually happen in one chain, with datawizard passing its result straight to ggplot2. The chain uses `|>` while it is still working on data and switches to `+` once `ggplot()` appears.

```r
euframes |>
  datawizard::data_filter(year >= 2009) |>
  datawizard::data_summary(mean_unemp = mean(unemp), by = "cntry") |>
  ggplot2::ggplot(ggplot2::aes(x = reorder(cntry, mean_unemp), y = mean_unemp)) +
  ggplot2::geom_col(fill = "#0e3b6a") +
  ggplot2::labs(x = NULL, y = "Mean unemployment, 2009–2013 (%)") +
  ggplot2::theme_minimal(base_size = 11)
```

`reorder()` sorts the country codes by the value being plotted rather than alphabetically, which turns a jumble of bars into a ranking you can read at a glance. `geom_col()` draws a bar whose height is the number stored in the data, which is what you want once `data_summary()` has already done the counting; its cousin `geom_bar()` counts the rows for you instead, and reaching for the wrong one of the two is a frequent small frustration.

Where two figures belong side by side, the **patchwork** package composes whole plots. `patchwork::wrap_plots(p1, p2)` sets two plot objects in a row, and `patchwork::wrap_plots(plots, nrow = 1)` does the same for a list of them; with the package attached by `library(patchwork)`, `p1 + p2` does it with the same `+` that adds layers.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Try it

Build a chain that keeps the crisis years, groups by `year`, and reports the mean of `mcosmo` and the mean of `mneg` per year, then pipe it into a plot with two `geom_line()` layers in different colours. You will find yourself wanting a legend and not getting one, because both colours were set rather than mapped. The remedy is to reshape the data into long form, with one row per year and outcome, using `data_to_long()` from datawizard (or `pivot_longer()` from tidyr), and then to map `colour` to the column that names the outcome.
:::

## 3. Reading the specification curve {#sec-speccurve}

The central figure of the course is a **specification curve**, and you now have every part needed to build one yourself. A hypothesis about a dataset admits many defensible analyses, and if you fit all of them and line the results up in order, you can see the range of answers that the data supports instead of the single answer that one analyst happened to report.

`data/spec_curve.csv` holds that curve for the EU-frames case: 864 rows, one per specification that the course judges a justifiable way of answering the claim, each recording the decisions that distinguish it from its neighbours, the partial correlation that it produced, and its p-values under several kinds of inference. The column `sig` records whether its p-value under standard errors clustered by country with the CR2 correction and Satterthwaite degrees of freedom lies below 0.05, the test that the course uses to class every point (the [statistics module](stats-methods.qmd#sec-inference) explains it), and `is_reference` marks the reference specification of the course, the analysis that analyst C6HJR submitted to Multi100, which is one of the three analyses that the one-day courses on the EU-frames case let you choose to reproduce in Task 3. Reading the file needs one preparatory step, which the paragraph after the code explains.

```r
curve <- readr::read_csv("data/spec_curve.csv") |>
  datawizard::data_modify(r_ca = dplyr::if_else(predictor == "growth", -r, r)) |>   # claim alignment
  datawizard::data_arrange("r_ca") |>
  datawizard::data_modify(rank = 1:n())

reference <- datawizard::data_filter(curve, is_reference)
```

The claim under test is that poor economic performance depresses the positive framing of the EU. With unemployment as the predictor, a negative correlation supports it, because a rise in unemployment is a worsening of the economy. With GDP growth as the predictor, support means a *positive* correlation instead, because a fall in growth is the worsening, and plotting the raw numbers together would scatter agreeing results on opposite sides of zero. **Claim alignment** repairs that. Flip the sign wherever the predictor is growth, and afterwards a negative value means support for every row alike. `if_else()` performs the flip, and the `_ca` suffix is the naming habit of the course for any claim-aligned quantity. The file already carries the aligned value in a column of the same name, so the line rebuilds something that you can check against the stored column. Sorting by the aligned value and numbering the rows then gives each specification a rank, and that rank becomes the horizontal axis.

```r
ggplot2::ggplot(curve, ggplot2::aes(x = rank, y = r_ca)) +
  ggplot2::geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linewidth = 0.4, colour = "#848c94") +
  ggplot2::geom_point(ggplot2::aes(shape = sig), size = 1.1, alpha = 0.5, colour = "#0e3b6a") +
  ggplot2::geom_point(data = reference, colour = "#8b1538", size = 3) +
  ggplot2::annotate(
    "text",
    x = reference$rank, y = reference$r_ca - 0.08,
    label = "the reference specification\n(C6HJR, t = -3.804)",
    colour = "#8b1538", fontface = "bold", size = 3.2, hjust = 1
  ) +
  ggplot2::scale_shape_manual(
    name   = NULL,
    values = c("TRUE" = 1, "FALSE" = 4),
    labels = c("TRUE" = "CR2 p < 0.05", "FALSE" = "CR2 p ≥ 0.05")
  ) +
  ggplot2::coord_cartesian(ylim = c(-0.65, 0.2)) +
  ggplot2::labs(
    x     = "specification, ranked by claim-aligned partial correlation",
    y     = "claim-aligned partial correlation",
    title = "The curve of the claim"
  ) +
  ggplot2::theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  ggplot2::theme(legend.position = "top", panel.grid.minor = ggplot2::element_blank())
```

Almost everything in that block has come up already: a reference line, a layer of small points whose shape is mapped to a logical column, a second point layer drawn from a *different* data frame, a manual scale, a zoom, labels and a theme. The manual scale sets the convention of the charts of the course, an open circle for a result below the 5% threshold and a cross for one above it, drawn at the same size and in translucent ink so that dense stretches of the curve stay readable and the class of a point is read from its shape rather than from a colour. `data = reference` inside the geom overrides the frame given to `ggplot()`, and that is how a single row gets picked out and emphasised. `annotate()` is the one function you have not met. It adds a mark that comes from no column at all, since you supply the coordinates and the text yourself, and that is why its position is read off `reference` rather than mapped.

Every point below the grey line is an analysis in the direction of the claim. Of the 864 specifications, 98.1% lie below it and 77.2% lie below it with a CR2 p-value under 0.05. The aligned correlations run from −0.589 to 0.116, so the curve holds firm support and a few results on the other side of zero. The burgundy point is the reference specification, the analysis that C6HJR submitted to Multi100, with a t-statistic of −3.804. Of the other specifications, 583 lie further below zero than it does, and with a CR2 p-value of 0.050 it is drawn as a cross. The submitted analysis was neither an outlier nor a cherry-pick, and yet the same menu, worked through in good faith by any competent analyst, would have produced a great many other numbers, most of them further in the direction of the claim.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Try it

Rebuild the curve, then add `colour = estimator` inside the `aes()` of the first point layer and delete the fixed `colour = "#0e3b6a"` that follows it, keeping the shapes as they are. The two colours largely separate along the ranking, which is why the estimator is the decision that moves the curve most, and the [Multiverse page](../cases/eu-frames/multiverse.qmd) explains what the two designs compare. Then try `ggplot2::facet_wrap(~ predictor)` on the same figure and ask yourself which of the two pictures you would rather a reviewer saw.
:::

## Sources and further study {#sec-sources}

This module was written for the course and adapts no existing lesson, so there is no borrowed text to attribute. It teaches only the part of R that the materials of the course use, in the order in which the course needs it.

The open resources for a fuller grounding in R are listed under [further study](https://codemoreh.github.io/ar4ds/tools/r.html#sec-sources) in Getting started with R. For the grammar of graphics, the chapters on visualisation in **"R for Data Science"**, the free book by the authors of the tidyverse packages, at <https://r4ds.hadley.nz/>, cover ggplot2 in full, and the documentation of the package, at [ggplot2.tidyverse.org](https://ggplot2.tidyverse.org/), is readable as an introduction as well as a reference.

When you are ready for a first statistical model, the module on [the statistical methods behind the course](stats-methods.qmd) takes the linear model on to the panel models that the EU-frames case requires.
